where: worked example 1, part (c), and quiz Q7
problem: The chapter states twice (Section 1 and Section 2) that slashing destroys part of the stake and removes the validator. The worked example then gives the slashed validator B a new chance of proposing (28.5% of the old total, 28.93% of the new total), and Q7 does the same. A removed validator has zero chance of proposing, so the example contradicts the rule the chapter just taught.
fix: Either say the example uses a design that applies a penalty but does not eject the validator: 'Suppose this chain applies a 5% penalty without ejection (some PoS designs do this)'. Or keep ejection and show it: B is removed, its chance becomes 0, and the other three share the remaining total. Use the same wording in Q7 so the two parts agree.

problem: Slashing is described only as signing two different blocks at the same height. Validators mostly sign attestations (votes), and signing two conflicting attestations is also a slashable offence, so a student may think only block proposers can be slashed.
fix: Say: 'a validator that signs two different blocks at the same height, or two conflicting attestations, loses part of its stake'.

problem: 'Cartel risk, because a few large stakers can coordinate' and 'DPoS uses fewer block producers, which can increase collusion risk' make the same point twice, which reads as two separate disadvantages.
fix: Merge into one bullet: 'Cartel risk: a few large stakers, or a small producer set, can coordinate to control block production.'

where: Section 3, disadvantage bullet on stake majority
problem: 'Security still needs an honest majority of stake' is vague and can mislead. A majority above one half is enough to control block production and censor, but finality in BFT-style PoS needs about two thirds of stake attesting; a student may read 'honest majority' as 51% being enough to break finality.
fix: Say: 'Security needs a large honest share of stake: above 50% an attacker can dominate block choice and censor, and finality rules usually need about two thirds of stake attesting.'

problem: 'a block can be declared final after two rounds or a fixed number of epochs' mixes two different things and does not say what a round is. In Casper-style designs a checkpoint is first justified and then finalised, one epoch apart.
fix: Say: 'In Casper-style designs a checkpoint is first justified, then finalised one epoch later, so finality takes two epochs.'
